paragraphs.text:
ON HERESIES, IN BRIEF

The mothers and prototypes of all heresies are four: 1. Barbarism, 2. Scythism, 3. Hellenism, 4. Judaism. From these all the others have sprung.

1. Barbarism: this stands by itself, having lasted from the days of Adam for ten generations, down to Noah. It is called Barbarism because the people of that time had no leader and no single agree-

-ment; instead each person kept to himself and became a law to himself, according to whatever his own will preferred.

2. Scythism: from the days of Noah and afterward until the building of the tower of Babylon, and for a few years after the time of the tower, that is, until Peleg [?] and Reu. These people turned toward the region of Europe and were assigned to the part of Scythia and its peoples, from the time of Tiras and after, from whom the Thracians descended.

3. Hellenism: this began with idolatry in the times of Serug. As each person at that time followed some superstition, the races of men began to be organized more along civic lines, into nations and the rites of idols. They deified those whom they had once followed. At first they depicted them in colours and made likenesses of those who were honoured among them at the time, whether tyrants, or sorcerers, or people who had done something in life that seemed worthy of remembrance, through valour or bodily strength. Then, from the times of Terah, the father of Abraham, who introduced idolatry, they fashioned images of their own dead, first by the potter's craft, then imitating them in every other craft: builders carved them from stone, silversmiths and goldsmiths fashioned them from their own materials, and likewise carpenters and the rest. The Egyptians, together with the Babylonians, the Phrygians and the Phoenicians, were the first to introduce this religion, with the making of statues and with mysteries. From them most of these things passed over to the Greeks from the age of Cecrops onward. Later, and much afterward, they proclaimed Cronus and Rhea, Zeus and Apollo, and the rest of the gods in turn as

gods. The Greeks are named after a certain Hellen, one of those who settled in Hellas, or, as others say, after the olive that sprouted at Athens. The Ionians became their leaders, as the precise account has it; they are named after Javan, one of the men who built the tower when the languages of all people were divided. For this reason they are all also called Meropes, because of the divided speech. Later on, Hellenism split into sects: I mean the Pythagoreans, the Stoics, the Platonists and the Epicureans. Meanwhile the character of godliness also existed, and the natural law was lived out, setting itself apart from these nations; from the foundation of the world onward it stood midway between Barbarism and Hellenism, until it was joined to the piety of Abraham.

4. Judaism: this received the mark of circumcision from the times of Abraham, and in Moses, the seventh from Abraham, it was put in writing through the law given by God. From Judah, the fourth son of Jacob, who was called Israel, and through David, the first to reign from that same tribe of Judah, it acquired its full name of Judaism. The Apostle clearly cut off these four when he said: "In Christ Jesus there is neither barbarian, nor Scythian, nor Greek, nor Jew, but a new creation."

The divisions of the Greeks:

5. Pythagoreans, or Peripatetics: Pythagoras taught the monad and providence. He forbade sacrificing to the so-called gods, and partaking of living creatures, and he taught abstinence from wine. He drew a distinction:

the things from the moon upward he called immortal, and the things below it mortal. He taught transmigrations of souls from body to body, even into animals and beasts. He also taught the practice of silence for a period of five years. In the end he named himself a god.

6. Platonists: they teach that God, matter and form exist, and that the world is created and perishable; that the soul is unbegotten, immortal and divine, and that it has three parts, the rational, the spirited and the desiring; that women should be common to all and no one should have a wife of his own, but men who wish may be with women who are willing. Likewise they teach the transmigration of souls into bodies, even into beasts. They also taught that many gods came from the one.

7. Stoics: they teach that the universe is body, and they consider this perceptible world to be God. Some of them declared that its nature comes from the substance of fire. They define God as mind, as the soul of the whole vessel of heaven and earth; its body, as I said, is the universe, and its eyes are the heavenly lights. They say that the flesh perishes and that the souls of all migrate from bodies into

8. Epicureans: they held that the first principle is atoms, indivisible bodies, uniform in their parts and infinite in number. They taught that the goal of happiness is pleasure, and that neither God nor providence governs affairs.

9. Samaritanism, and the Samaritans who derive from it. It derives from the Jews. It arose before sects had formed among the Greeks and before their doctrines had taken shape, but after the religion of the Greeks already existed, and in the midst of Judaism. It took its occasion from the times of Nebuchadnezzar and the

captivity of the Jews. They were settlers brought from Assyria into Judea, and they received the Pentateuch of Moses, which the king sent them from Babylon through a priest called Ezra. They keep everything as the Jews do, except that they abhor the gentiles and will not touch anyone, and except that they deny the resurrection of the dead and the other prophecies after Moses.

The Samaritan sects, four:

10. Gorthenes: they celebrate their festivals at different times from the Sebuaeans.

11. Sebuaeans: they differ with the Gorthenes over the festivals.

12. Essenes: they oppose neither group, but celebrate the festivals indifferently with whichever they happen to be among.

13. Dositheans: they live by the same customs as the Samaritans, practising circumcision and the rest, and using the Pentateuch. But more than the others they keep abstinence from living creatures, and likewise from other things, and they live in almost constant fasting. They also practise virginity; some of them practise continence; and others believe in the resurrection of the dead, which is foreign to the Samaritans.

The Jewish sects, seven:

14. Scribes: they were lawyers and repeaters of the traditions of their elders. Through excessive self-chosen worship they kept customs which they had not learned from the law, but had devised for themselves as objects of reverence and ordinances, outside the

15. Pharisees, which is translated "separated ones": they live in the strictest way and are supposedly more approved than the others. Among them there is belief in the resurrection of the dead, as also among the Scribes, and assent concerning angels and the Holy Spi-

-rit, that they exist. They have a distinctive way of life, continence [?] and virginity for a period, fasting twice a week, purifications of pots, platters and cups, as the Scribes also have; tithes and firstfruits, continual prayers, and self-chosen styles of dress, such as the cloak and the dalmatics, that is, the colobia; and the broadening of the phylacteries, that is, the bands of purple; and the fringes and pomegranate-shaped tassels on the edges of the cloak, which served among them as signs of a season of continence. They also introduced nativity and fate.

16. Sadducees, which is translated "most righteous": they were of Samaritan stock, and were named after a priest named Zadok. They deny the resurrection of the dead and do not accept either angel or spirit; but in all else they are Jews.

17. Hemerobaptists: they were Jews in every respect, but said that no one obtains eternal life unless he is baptized every day [?].

18. Ossenes, whose name is translated [?] "most shameless": they did everything according to the law. But they used other scriptures besides the law, and rejected most of the later prophets.

19. Nasaraeans, which is translated "unruly": they forbid all eating of meat, and do not partake of living creatures at all. As far as Moses and

Joshua son of Nun, they use the holy names of the patriarchs in the Pentateuch and believe in them; I mean Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and those before them, and Moses himself, and Aaron and Joshua. But they teach that the scriptures of the Pentateuch are not by Moses, and they maintain that there are others besides these.

20. Herodians: they were Jews in every respect, but they expected Herod as the Christ, and gave him the honour and the name of Christ.

Here [?] is the first [?] volume, containing [?] the twenty heresies [?]; in it is also an account of the coming of Christ [?].

21. Simonians: these come from Simon the magician, who lived in the time of Peter the Apostle, from the village of Gitta in Samaria. [?] He came from the Samaritans and assumed only the name of Christian. He taught shameful intercourse, defilement and indifference about bodies. He rejects the resurrection and says that the world is not God's. He gave his disciples an image of himself as Zeus, and of the harlot who was with him, named Helen, in the form of Athena, for them to worship. He said that he himself was the Father to the Samaritans and the Christ to the Jews.

22. Menandrians: these began from Simon through a certain Menander, but differed from the Simonians in some respect. They said that the world [was made] by angels

23. Saturnilians: in Syria they reinforced the obscenity of the Simonians, but preached other things besides the Simonians, to cause still greater astonishment. They take their origin from Saturnilus. Like Menander, they too say that the world came into being by angels, but by seven only, [?] the will of the Father.

24. Basilidians: of the same obscenity [?] placed a power outside the world, which [he called] "Depth and Silence" [?] and quiet,

[?] practitioners, from Basilides, who was a disciple along with Saturnilus, the Simonians and the Menandrians, and held similar views but differed in some respect. For he says there are 365 heavens, and gives them the names of angels. This is why the year has that many days; and the name Abrasax adds up to 365, and he says that this is a holy name.

25. Nicolaitans: these come from Nicolaus, who was appointed by the apostles over the daily needs. Out of jealousy over his own wife he taught his disciples to practise obscenity along with the others, and he introduced into the world [talk] about Kaulakau and Prunicus and other barbarous names.

26. Gnostics: they took over the heresies,

but practise obscenity more madly than all of these. In Egypt they are called Stratiotics and Phibionites, in the upper regions Socratites [?], and among others Zacchaeans. Some call them Coddians, and others call them Borborites. They boast of Barbelo [?] and Bero.

27. Carpocratians: these come from a certain Carpocrates, one of those in Asia. He taught people to commit every obscenity and every kind of sin. Unless someone, he says, passes through everything and does the will of all the demons and angels, he cannot rise above the highest heaven, nor pass the Principalities and Authorities. He said that Jesus received an intelligent soul, and that, knowing the things above, he proclaimed [?] them here; and that whoever does things like Jesus is equal to him. He rejected the law along with the resurrection of the dead, as did those from Simon and the heresies up to this point. From him came Marcellina in Rome; she made images of Jesus, Paul, Homer and Pythagoras in secret, and burned incense to them and worshipped them.

28. Cerinthians, also called Merinthians: these come from Cerinthus and Merinthus, certain Jews who boasted of circumcision. They said that the world came into being by angels, and that Jesus was called Christ by advancement. [?] taught to worship these; but by emendation [?]. Reg. 2508: "but by advancement Christ [?]"

[?]

29. Nazoraeans: they confess Christ Jesus, the Son of God, but live in every respect according to the law.

30. Ebionites: they resemble the Cerinthians and Nazoraeans mentioned above. Joined to them in some respect is the heresy of the Sampsaeans and Elkesaites, who say that Christ was created in heaven, and the Holy Spirit too; that Christ came to dwell in Adam, and from time to time put off Adam himself and put him on again; and they say that he did the same thing in his coming in the flesh. Although they are Jews, they use the Gospels. They abhor the eating of meat. They regard water as God. They say that in his coming in the flesh Christ put on a man, as I said. They are continually baptized in water, summer and winter, supposedly for purification, like the Samaritans.

31. Valentinians: they reject

the resurrection of the flesh and set aside the Old Testament, though they read the prophets and accept whatever else can be allegorized to resemble their heresy. They bring in other mythologies, speaking of the names of thirty aeons, male and female together, born from the Father of all, whom they regard both as gods and as aeons. They say that Christ brought his flesh from heaven and passed through Mary as through a pipe.

32. Secundians: with them are associated Epiphanes and Isidore. They use the same pairs of aeons and hold the same views as Valentinus, but relate some other things somewhat differently from them. They too reject the flesh.

33. Ptolemaeans: they are disciples and [?] of Valen-

-tinus. Flora is associated with them. These too say the same things about the pairs of aeons as the Valentinians and Secundians, but they also differ in some respect.

This is also the summary of the second volume of the first book, of the thirteen. These are contained in this [?] volume, in which there are thirteen heresies.

34. Marcosians: a certain Mark was a fellow student of Colorbasus, and he too introduces two principles. He rejects the resurrection of the dead. He produced certain illusions with cups, changing them by incantation to a blue and a purple colour, and so initiated the women he deceived. Like Valentinus, he too would have all things governed by the twenty-four letters.

35. Colorbasians: [?] this Colorbasus likewise relates the same things, but differs in some respect from the other heresies, I mean from those of Mark and Valentinus. He taught the emanations and ogdoads differently.

36. Heracleonites: these too appear to follow the mythology of the ogdoads, though differently from Mark, Ptolemy, Valentinus and the rest. Moreover, at the point of death they "redeem" their dying, as Mark does, with oil, balsam and water, pronouncing certain invocations in Hebrew words over the head of the one who is supposedly being redeemed.

37. Ophites: they glorify the serpent and regard it as Christ, and they keep a [?] snake, the reptile itself, in a kind of box.

38. Cainites: like the other heresies that reject the law and the one who spoke in the law, they hold the same views. They deny the resurrection of the flesh, but glorify Cain, saying that he is of the stronger power. They also deify Judas, along with Korah, Dathan and Abiram and their company, and the Sodomites.

39. Sethians: these in turn glorify Seth. They say that he is from the Mother above, who repented of having produced Cain and his kind. Then, after Cain had been cast out and Abel slain, she united with the Father above and produced Seth as a pure seed, from whom the whole human race was afterward derived. These too teach doctrines of principalities and authorities and the rest.

40. Archontics: these in turn trace everything back to many archons, and say that created things came into being from them. They are also caught in a certain obscenity. They reject the resurrection of the flesh and reject the Old Testament. Yet they use the Old and the New Testament, twisting every word to their own meaning.

41. Cerdonians: these come from Cerdo, who took over his share of the error from Heracleon and added to the deceit. He moved from Syria to Rome and set out his preaching in the time of Bishop Hyginus. He preaches two principles opposed to each other, and that Christ was not born. Likewise he rejects the resurrection of the dead and the Old Testament. Unless he lays curses against [?]

originating [?], the son of a bishop, he seduced a virgin and fled, because he had been expelled from the Church by his own father. He went up to Rome and then asked for repentance from those who were leading the Church at that time; failing to obtain it, he rose up against the faith and taught three principles, the good, the just and the evil, and that the New Testament is foreign to the Old and to the one who spoke in it. He and the Marcionists who came from him reject the resurrection of the flesh, and they give baptism not only once, but twice and three times, after someone has lapsed. Among them, others are baptized on behalf of the dead and of catechumens. Among them women are also freely permitted to administer the washing.

43. Lucianists: a certain Lucian, not the one who lived recently in the times of Constantine but an older one, taught everything as Marcion did. Besides this, they also supposedly teach some other things beyond Marcion.

44. Apelleans: this Apelles too teaches things similar to Marcion and Lucian. He reviles the whole creation and its maker. Unlike them, however, he did not set forth three principles, but one principle and one God, who is highest and cannot be named; and this one God made another. And this one who came into being, he says, turned out to be evil, and made the world in his wickedness.

45. Severians: a certain Severus [?], following on from Apelles, rejects wine, and [says] that the vine sprang from the serpent-like Satan and the earth [?] Reg. 2508: "in the beginning of elements and numbers, God"; God [?] Marcion [?] disciple of Saturninus [?] (30) Severus [?] Tatian a little later [?]

[?] when they came together. He rejects woman, saying that she belongs to the left-hand power. He brings in certain names of archons and apocryphal books. Like the others, he rejects the resurrection of the flesh and the Old Testament.

46. Tatianists: this Tatian flourished at the same time as Justin, the most holy martyr and philosopher. After the death of Saint Justin he was further corrupted by the doctrines of Marcion, and taught the same things as he did, adding other things besides. He was said to come from Mesopotamia [?].

These are the heresies of the first volume of the second book: thirteen. Contained in the third volume of the second book are eighteen heresies.

47. Encratites: they are an offshoot of Tatian. They reject marriage, saying that it is of Satan, and they forbid all eating of living creatures.

48. [The heresy] of the Cataphrygians, Montanists
and Ascodrugites: they accept the Old and the New Testament, but bring in other prophets, boasting of a certain Montanus and Priscilla.

49. Pepuzians, also called Quintillians, with whom the Artotyrites are associated: two heresies. They come from the Cataphrygians themselves, but teach other things besides. They deify Pepuza, a city between Galatia, Cappadocia and Phrygia, and regard it as Jerusalem, although there is also another Pepuza. They give women the right to rule and to serve as priests. They perform a certain initiation in which they pierce a young child all over with bronze needles, as the Cataphrygians do, knead flour with its blood, make bread of it, and partake of it as an offering. They also tell the tale that Christ was revealed there in Pepuza to Quintilla or Priscilla in female form. They likewise use the Old and the New

BOOK ON HERESIES. …Testament, reshaping it to suit their own understanding. 50. Quartodecimans: they celebrate the Pascha on a single day of the year, on whatever day the fourteenth of the moon happens to fall, whether on a Sabbath or on a Lord's day. They fast on that day and also keep vigil as they celebrate it. 51. Alogi, as we have named them: they reject the Gospel according to John and his Revelation, because they do not accept God the Word, who came from the Father and who always is. 52. Adamians: named after a certain Adam who is living [?], they hold a doctrine fit for mockery rather than one of truth. What happens among them is something like this: men and women gather in the same place naked, as they came from their mothers, and in this state they perform the readings, the prayers and everything else they do. They supposedly live as monks, practise continence and do not accept marriage, and they consider their church to be paradise. 53. Sampsaeans, also called Elkesaites: they still live today in Arabia, which lies above the Dead Sea. They were deceived by Elxai, a false prophet. Women of his family, Marthus and Marthina, were still living in our own day and were worshipped by the sect as goddesses. In every respect they are like the Ebionites. 54. Theodotians: the followers of Theodotus the leather-worker

from Byzantium. He became outstanding in Greek learning, but in the days of the persecution at that time he alone fell away, along with others [?], while the rest were martyred for God's sake. Because he was reproached for having fled in this way, he devised the teaching that Christ was a mere man, on account of the charge that he had denied God. 55. Melchizedekians: these honour Melchizedek, claiming that he is a certain power and not merely a mere man, and they have dared to refer everything to his name. 56. Bardesanists: this Bardesanes came from Mesopotamia. At first he belonged to the true faith and was distinguished in philosophy. But he turned aside from the truth and taught doctrines similar to those of Valentinus, apart from a few points on which he differs from Valentinus. 57. Noetians: this Noetus was from Smyrna in Asia. Puffed up [?] along with others, he called Christ a 'Son-Father' and taught that the same one is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. He said that he himself was Moses and that his brother was Aaron.

…are those who live in Bacathus, a chief village of Philadelphia in Arabia. They castrate those who come across them and stay with them as guests, and most of them are themselves eunuchs, having been cut. They teach various other things full of heresy, rebelling against the Law and the prophets and bringing in certain other obscenities. 59. Cathari: these joined with Novatus the Roman. They reject those who have married a second time altogether, and they do not accept repentance. 60. Angelics: these have died out completely. They boasted that they held the rank of angels, or else they were so called because they called upon angels.

61. Apostolics, also called Apotactics: these too are found only around Pisidia, and they accept only those who have renounced their possessions. They are close to the Encratites, but on other points they think differently from them. 62. Sabellians: they hold views similar to those of Noetus, except that they say the Father did not suffer. They say that he was uttered forth [?] and then drawn back again [?]

…these are obscene, committing unspeakable acts and handing their own bodies over to corruption. 64. Origenists, a different group, followers of Origen, also called Adamantius, the writer: they reject the resurrection of the dead and teach that Christ and the Holy Spirit are creatures. They allegorize paradise, the heavens and everything else. They babble that the kingdom of Christ will one day come to an end and that the angels will come to an end along with it. They tell the absurd tale that Christ will reign [?] together with the devil, and that Christ was crucified by demons. These are the eighteen heresies of the fourth tome of the second book. The fifth tome of the second book contains five heresies. 65. Paulianists: from Paul of Sa-

mosata. This Paul all but affirms that Christ did not exist. He fashions him into an uttered word and holds that he exists from Mary onward. On this view, what the divine Scriptures say about him was said as an advance announcement of one who was foretold but did not yet exist, and he has his existence only from Mary onward, from his coming in the flesh. 66. Manichaeans, also called Acuanites: these are disciples of Manes the Persian. They speak of Christ as existing only in appearance. They worship the sun and the moon and pray to stars, powers and demons. They teach two principles, one evil and one good, both always existing. They say that Christ appeared and suffered only in semblance. They blaspheme the Old Testament and the God who spoke in it, and they hold that not the whole world but only a part of it came into being from God. 67. Hieracites: these come from Hierax of Leontopolis in Egypt, a certain interpreter of Scripture. They reject the resurrection of the flesh but use the Old and New Testaments. They forbid marriage altogether and accept monks, virgins, the continent
in these words: 'Let him write to Artemas, and let those who follow Artemas be in communion with him.' This man (Paul) to [?]
…was said [?] to stir up: 'Since the air is the soul of human beings, of animals, of birds and of fish,'

and widows. They say that children who die before reaching maturity have no share in the kingdom, because they have not run the contest. 68. Meletians: they are a schism in Egypt, not a heresy. They would not pray with those who had lapsed during the persecutions. Now, however, they have joined the Arians. 69. Arians, also called Ariomanites and Diatomites: they say that the Son of God is a creature and that the Holy Spirit is a creature of a creature. They affirm that Christ took only flesh from Mary and not a soul as well. These are the five heresies of the fifth tome of the second book. The first tome of the third book contains six heresies. 70. Audians: a schism and a rebellion, but not a heresy. Their conduct and way of life are well ordered, and in every respect they hold the same faith as the Catholic Church. Most of them live in monasteries, and they do not pray with everyone. They make much use of apocryphal writings, and they lavish criticism on our bishops for being rich, and on others for other things. They celebrate the Pascha on their own [?]

…along with the Jews. They also have a peculiar and contentious notion, interpreting 'in the image' in the most literal way. 71. Photinians: this Photinus came from Sirmium. He held views similar to those of Paul of Samosata, though he differed from him on some point. He too affirms that Christ exists from Mary onward. 72. Marcellians: followers of Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia. At first he was rumoured to hold views similar to Sabellius. He came forward many times to defend himself and also defended himself in writing, but others accused him of persisting in the same views. Perhaps he changed his mind and set himself right, or else his disciples did. For some orthodox people acted as mediators and spoke in defence of his words. 73. Semi-Arians: they confess that Christ is a creature, but they call him a creature disingenuously, not as one of the creatures. 'Rather,' they say, 'we call him Son, but we call him created so as not to attach passion to the Father by his having begotten.' In the same way they declare that the Holy Spirit is entirely a creature. They reject the term 'consubstantial' for the Son and prefer to say 'of like substance.' Some of them have rejected even 'of like substance.'
…from Theodore and from Diodore, Diodorians [?] (Cod. S. Hil.) [?] the second council.

74. Pneumatomachi: These speak rightly about Christ, with some reservation [?], but they blaspheme the Holy Spirit. They define him as created and as not being of the Godhead. Rather, they say, he was created in a loose sense through an activity [?], and they claim that he is only a sanctifying power. 75. Aerians: This Aerius came from Pontus and is still alive today, a trial to the world. He was a presbyter under Bishop Eustathius, who was accused of Arianism. Because this Aerius was not made a bishop, he taught many things against the Church. In faith he is a thoroughgoing Arian, but he goes further and teaches that offerings must not be made for those who have fallen asleep. He forbids fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays, and keeping Lent and the Pascha. He preaches renunciation, yet he eats every kind of meat and food without scruple. If any of his followers wants to fast, he tells him to do so not on appointed days but whenever he likes, 'for,' he says, 'you are not under the law.' He claims that presbyters do not differ at all from a bishop.

76. Aetians: the followers of Aetius the Cilician, who was ordained deacon by George, the Arian bishop of Alexandria. They are also called Anomoeans, and some call them Eunomians, after a certain Eunomius who became a disciple of Aetius. Eudoxius was also associated with them, but supposedly out of fear of the emperor Constantine he separated himself from them, and Aetius alone was banished. Eudoxius, however, remained an Arian, though not after the fashion of Aetius. These Anomoeans and Aetians completely estrange Christ and the Holy Spirit from God the Father. They affirm that he is created, and they say he does not have even any likeness to the Father. They try to present God by means of Aristotelian and geometrical syllogisms, and by such reasoning to show that Christ supposedly cannot be from God. The Eunomians who came from them rebaptize everyone who comes over to them, not only [others] but also those who come from the Arians, turning the baptized upside down, feet up and head down, as the story widely goes. They say that falling into anything, fornication or any other sin, is no great matter, for God requires nothing except that one hold this faith of theirs. These, then, are likewise the seven heresies of the first tome of the third book. In the second [tome] of the third book, heresies [?]. 77. Dimoerites, also called Apollinarians: those who do not
Cod. S. Hil.: Aetians, also called Anomoeans, and Eunomians, and Eudoxians.

confess that Christ's coming, that is, his becoming man, was complete. Some of them once dared to say that his body was consubstantial with the Godhead. Some at one time said that he also took a soul, and at another time denied this [?]. Others, relying on the saying 'The Word became flesh,' denied that he took flesh from created flesh, that is, from Mary, and contentiously maintained only that the Word became flesh. Later, with I know not what in mind, they said that he did not take a mind. 78. Antidicomarianites: they say that holy Mary, the ever-virgin, had marital relations with Joseph after giving birth to the Saviour. 79. Collyridians: on a certain appointed day of the year they offer a kind of bread-cake (a collyris) in the name of this same Mary; for this reason we have given them the name Collyridians. 80. Massalians, a name that means 'Euchites' (those who pray).

BOOK ON HERESIES. Joined to these are also the so-called Euphemites, Martyrians and Satanians, from among the heresies devised by the pagans. This is the summary of the seventh tome. Chapters of the impious doctrine of the Massalians, taken from their book. 1. That Satan dwells substantially in man and rules over him in everything. 2. That Satan and the demons hold possession of the human mind, and that human nature is in communion with the spirits of wickedness. 3. That Satan and the Holy Spirit dwell together in man, and that not even the apostles were free of the working of the demon. 4. That baptism does not perfect a person, nor does partaking of the divine mysteries cleanse the soul, but only the [prayer] diligently practised among them

5. That even after baptism a person remains mingled with sin. 6. That the believer receives the incorruptible and divine garment not through baptism but through prayer [?]. 7. That one must also receive freedom from passion and participation in the Holy Spirit with full perception, and come to full assurance.

8. That the soul must perceive its communion with the heavenly Bridegroom in the same way that a woman perceives her husband in intercourse. 9. That spiritual people see, both within and without, sin and grace at work and being worked. 10. That there is a revelation which comes about with perception and in divine substance, as a doctrine. 11. That fire is creative. 12. That the soul which does not have Christ with perception and in every working is a dwelling-place of serpents and venomous beasts, that is, of every hostile power. 13. That evils exist by nature. 14. That even before the transgression Adam had intercourse with Eve [?] without passion. 15. That seed and Word fell into Mary. 16. That a person must acquire two souls, they say: one that is common to human beings, and one that is heavenly. 17. That, they say, a person can receive the substance of the Holy Spirit perceptibly, with full assurance and full working. 18. That the Saviour can be made manifest in light to those who pray, and that at one time a man was found standing by the altar, and three loaves kneaded with oil were offered to him. Moreover, they also turn away from manual labour as unfitting for Christians. In part they also introduce inhumanity towards the poor. They claim that it is not fitting for those who have renounced the world, or who are just beginning to do good at all, to give help to those who beg in public, or to widows who have been left destitute, or to people who have met with misfortune, whether bodily injury, illness, harsh creditors, raids by robbers or barbarians, or any other such calamity; rather, everything should be supplied to themselves. For they claimed that they themselves were the ones who are truly poor in spirit. To this they added contempt for the churches and altars, on the grounds that ascetics ought not to attend the church assemblies but should be content with the prayers in their own houses of prayer. For they said that the power of prayer is so great that the Holy Spirit appears perceptibly both to themselves and to those they have made disciples. They spin the fantastic tale that those who wish to be saved must keep on praying, doing nothing else whatever, until they perceive sin like smoke, or fire, or a dragon, or some

such beast, being driven out by their prayer and departing perceptibly through their prayers; and until they in turn perceptibly receive the entry of the Holy Spirit and have a clear perception in the soul of the Spirit's entry. This, they say, is the true communion of Christians. For those who are baptized do not by any means receive the Holy Spirit in the Church's baptism or in the ordinations of clergy, unless they take part more diligently in their prayers. And a person could receive communion of the Holy Spirit even without baptism, if he were willing to stay with them and be instructed in their doctrines. Thus, when presbyters told them, 'We confess that we have the Holy Spirit by faith, not by perception,' they promised that perception of the Spirit would be imparted to them too through prayer together with them. The conceit of their arrogance is so great that those who have supposedly received perception of the Spirit among them are called blessed by them as perfect, free of all sin and superior, and are attended and revered as no longer subject to the dangers of sin. Instead, from then on they are allowed ease, freedom in what they eat, and every kind of escort, honour and luxury. Yet many of them, even after receiving such testimony to their perfection from them, have been found among outsiders unworthy even to be called Christians, having fallen into various obscenities, thefts of money and fornications.

In addition to what has been said, they tell many other fantastic tales. For example, they dissolve lawful marriages with the utmost indifference, and they receive and call blessed, as ascetics, those who abandon their marriages. They persuade fathers and mothers to neglect the raising of their children, and they coax them into bringing everything to themselves. They readily take in slaves who run away from their masters. To sinners who come to them they promise speedy cleansing from every sin, without any fruit of repentance, without the authority of a priest, and without the stages laid down in the Church's canons, provided only that the person practises their much-vaunted prayer with them and becomes a hastily made initiate of their trickery. As a result they even bring some such people to ordination as clergy before they have been released from their sins, craftily persuading the bishops to lay hands on them; the bishops are lured by the testimony of those whom they regard as ascetics. They are eager for this, not because they consider the clerical ranks honourable, since they despise even the bishops themselves whenever they please, but because they are seeking some power and authority for themselves. Some of them

say that they should not even partake of the mysteries unless they perceptibly sense the presence of the Spirit, coming upon them at that very hour. Some of them allow those who wish to cut off their own genitals. They also casually disregard excommunications. They swear oaths and perjure themselves without scruple, and they deceitfully anathematize their own heresy. More on the aforesaid heresy of the Massalians, who are found especially in monasteries, from the History of Theodoret. In the time of Valentinian and Valens the heresy of the Massalians sprang up. Those who translate the name into Greek call them Euchites. They also have another name, which comes from what they do: they are called Enthusiasts, because they receive the working of a demon and take it to be the Holy Spirit. Those who have taken in the disease to its full extent turn away from manual labour as wicked; they give themselves over to sleep and call the fantasies of their dreams 'inspiration'. The leaders of this heresy were Dadoes, Sabas, Adelphius, Hermas, Simeon and others besides, who withdrew from the communion of the Church, claiming that the divine food neither helps nor harms, the food of which Christ says, 'Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will live for ever.' Yet they try to hide their disease, and even after being exposed they shamelessly deny it and denounce those who hold the very views that they carry about in their own souls. However, a certain Letoius, who governed the church of Melitene and was adorned with divine zeal, saw many monasteries, or rather dens of robbers, that had contracted this disease. He burned them down and drove the wolves out of the flock. Likewise the all-praised Amphilochius, who had been entrusted with the metropolis of the Lycaonians and governed that whole people, learned that this plague had broken out there; he too rose up and freed the flocks he tended from that corruption. And Flavian, the renowned high priest of the Antiochenes, learned that they were living in Edessa and pouring out their venom on those who came near them. He sent a band of monks, brought them to Antioch, and exposed them, though they denied the disease, in the following way. He said that their accusers were slandering them and that the witnesses were lying. Then he gently bade Adelphius, who was very old, to sit beside him, and said: 'Old man, we who have lived the longer part of life have come to know human nature more precisely,

and we have recognized the wrongdoings of the hostile demons, and we have learned by experience the gift of grace. But these men are young and know none of these things precisely, so they cannot bear to hear more spiritual words. So tell me, how do you say that the opposing spirit withdraws and the grace of the all-holy Spirit comes upon a person?' Charmed by these words, the old man vomited up all his hidden venom. He said that baptism brings no benefit to those who receive it, and that only earnest prayer drives out the indwelling demon. For, he said, everyone who is born draws from the forefather slavery to the demons, just as he draws his nature. When these are driven out by earnest prayer, the all-holy Spirit then comes, signalling his presence perceptibly and visibly. He frees the body from the stirrings of the passions and delivers the soul completely from its inclination towards what is worse, so that from then on there is no further need of fasting to subdue the body, nor of teaching to rein it in and train it to walk in good order. And the one who has attained this is not only freed from the leapings of the body, but also clearly foresees the future and beholds the divine Trinity with his eyes. When the divine Flavian had thus broken open the foul-smelling spring and made him lay bare his thoughts, he said to the impious old man: 'You who have grown old in evil days, your own mouth has convicted you, and not I; your own lips have testified against you.' Once this disease had been exposed, they were driven out of Syria. They withdrew to Pamphylia and filled that land with their corruption too. These are the heresies up to Marcian. From Marcian onward, a little before [?] and under Leo, the following heresies sprang up. 81. Nestorians: who separately and divided-

[?] teaching that God the Word exists separately and his man separately. They attribute the humbler of the things the Lord did during his sojourn among us to his man alone, and the loftier, God-befitting ones to God the Word alone, and do not ascribe both together to one and the same person. 82. Eutychianists, who take the name of their heresy from Eutyches. They do not say that our Lord Jesus Christ took flesh from the holy Virgin Mary, but declare that he became incarnate in some more divine way. They have not grasped that the one whom God the Word united to himself from the Virgin Mary was man, liable for the sin of their forefather Adam. Through that same man, as it is written, he stripped off the principalities and powers and made a public example of them, triumphing over them on the cross. He had put on those powers through the transgression of the first-formed man.

83 [?]. Egyptians, also called Schematics and Monophysites. On the pretext of the document of Chalcedon, the Tome [?], they split away from the Orthodox Church. They are called Egyptians because Egyptians were the first to start this schism, under the emperors Marcian and Valentinian. In all other respects they are orthodox. These, out of

partiality toward Dioscorus of Alexandria, who was deposed by the synod of Chalcedon for championing the doctrines of Eutyches, set themselves against the synod and invented countless charges against it on that account. We have already refuted these charges sufficiently in the present book, showing the Egyptians to be perverse and vain-minded. Their leaders were Theodosius of Alexandria, from whom come the Theodosians, and James the Syrian, from whom come the Jacobites. Their accomplices, confirmers and champions were Severus, the corrupter of Antioch, and John the Tritheite, whose labours were in vain. These men deny the mystery of our common salvation. They wrote much against the divinely inspired teaching of the six hundred and thirty Fathers at Chalcedon. Besides their destructive heresy, they have set many stumbling blocks for those who are perishing: "snares," as the saying goes, and "stumbling blocks beside the path." Moreover, by teaching particular substances they confound the mystery of the economy. We have thought it necessary to treat their impiety in summary, adding some brief notes to refute their godless and utterly foul heresy. I shall set out the doctrines, or rather the drivel, of their champion John, which they take special pride in.

On nature and hypostasis: what the followers of Severus believe, and how they teach particular substances. From John the Grammarian, the Tritheite, called Philoponus, from the [?] discourse of the [?].

The common and universal definition of human nature is one in itself. Yet when it comes to be in many subjects it becomes many, existing wholly in each of them and not partially. In the same way, the design of a ship in the shipwright is one, but it is multiplied when it comes to be in many subjects. So too the theorem in the teacher is one in its own definition, but when it comes to be in the learners it is multiplied along with them, coming to be whole in each. Further, the device on a signet ring is one, but it comes to be whole in each of many wax impressions, and from then on it both is many and is called many. So the many ships, the many men, the many impressions and the thoughts in the many pupils are more than one in number as individuals; in that respect they are divided and not united. But in the common form the many men are one, and the many ships are one. The same is true of the thoughts, and the impressions have their oneness in the sameness of the imprint. So these things are many and divided in one respect, and united and one in another. Even with continuous things we often apply number,

saying, for example, that a piece of wood is two cubits long. But we say that the one thing is two potentially, not actually, since in actuality it is one and not two. Because it can be cut and become two, in that sense we say it is of two cubits.

From the Arbiter. The seventh argument is the one that confirms its own truth from what those who hold the opposite view propose. They propose that Christ's natures are two, yet claim that his hypostasis, that is, his person, is one and only one. At the same time they reject those who hold either that Christ's nature after the union is one or that his hypostases are two. Before we launch into refuting this position, I think it reasonable first to define what the teaching of the Churches means by the term "nature," and what by "person" and "hypostasis." By nature it means the common definition of being shared by things that partake of the same substance. For every man, for example, this is "a rational, mortal animal, capable of mind and knowledge," and in this no man differs from another. It treats substance and nature as the same. By hypostasis, or person, it means the self-subsistent existence of each nature and, so to speak, its circumscription, made up of certain properties by which those who share the same nature differ from one another. In short, it means what the Peripatetics like to call individuals, in which the division of the common genera and species comes to an end. These the teachers of the Church called hypostases, and sometimes also persons. Animal is divided into rational and irrational, and rational again into man, angel and demon. The things into which each of these lowest species is finally cut, as man into Peter and Paul, or angel into, say, Gabriel and Michael and each of the other angels, are called individuals. This is because none of them can be cut further into other things and still keep its one nature after the cutting: dividing a man into soul and body destroys the whole. Hence the philosophers like to call these individuals. The language of the Church, however, named such things hypostases, because in them genera and species receive their existence. Animal, for instance, is a genus and man a species, and each has its own definition of being. Yet they have their existence in individuals such as Peter and Paul, and do not subsist apart from them. We have now stated, according to the teaching of the Church, what a hypostasis is and what a nature is.

This common nature, then, the nature of man, by which no man differs from any other, comes to be in each of the individuals. Once there, it becomes proper to that one individual and common to no one else, as we defined in the fourth chapter. The rational, mortal animal in me is common to no other animal. When a man, an ox or a horse suffers, it is perfectly possible for the other individuals of the same species to remain unaffected. When Paul has died, it may be that none of the other men has died; and when Peter came to be and was brought into existence, the men who came after him were not yet among the things that exist. So each nature is spoken of in two ways, not one. In one way, we consider the common definition of each nature by itself, such as the nature of man or of horse, as existing in none of the individuals. In the other, we see this same common nature existing in the individuals, receiving in each of them a most particular existence and fitting no one else but that one alone. The rational, mortal animal in me is common to none of the other men, and the nature of animal in this horse could not come to be in any other, as we have just shown. The teaching of the Church plainly holds these notions about natures and hypostases. We confess one nature of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, but teach three hypostases, that is, persons, each distinguished from the others by some property. What would the one nature of the Godhead be, if not the common definition of the divine nature considered by itself and separated in thought from the property of each hypostasis? We also understand the term "nature" in a more particular sense: we regard the common definition of the nature as having become proper to each of the individuals, that is, to each of the hypostases, and as no longer able to fit any other member of the common species. This again is clear from the fact that in Christ we profess a union of two natures, the divine and the human. We do not say that the common nature of the Godhead, as understood in the Holy Trinity, became incarnate, for then we would also be asserting the incarnation of the Holy Spirit. Nor do we hold that the common definition of human nature was united to God the Word. If it were, the Word of God could rightly be said to have been united to all the men who lived before the Word's sojourn among us and all who will live after it. Clearly, then, by the nature of the Godhead we mean here the nature of the common Godhead in the hypostasis of the Word. That is why we also confess "one incarnate nature of God the Word": by adding "of God the Word" we clearly distinguish it from the Father and the Holy Spirit. So here too we understand the common definition of the divine nature as having become proper to the divine Word, and say that the nature of God the Word became incarnate. And again, when we say that the nature of humanity was united to the Word, we mean that most particular existence which alone out of

all the Word assumed. In this sense of "nature," then, nature and hypostasis would be almost the same. The only difference is that the term "hypostasis" also includes in its meaning the properties that each acquires beyond the common nature, by which they are separated from one another. That is why many of our own writers can be found saying indifferently that a union of natures, that is, of hypostases, took place. Hypostasis, as we have shown, signifies the particular and individual existence of each thing. Since they often use these terms interchangeably, they clearly mean the most particular nature by them. In everyday conversation too, and in the usage of those who have studied the nature of such things, everyone customarily calls the common definition of the nature "man," as when they say that man is a species of animal, since no individual either is or is called a species under the genus. We also say that man differs from horse, meaning of course the universal natures themselves. And again we say that Peter is a man, and Paul, and John, and that a man was born and died, meaning of course the particular one, while the common definition of human nature remains as it was. It is also reasonable to make this distinction beforehand. Among us the terms "person" and "hypostasis" often indicate the same meaning, just as one might call the same thing both "sword" and "blade." Thus in the case of the Holy Trinity we speak indifferently of three persons and three hypostases, using each term interchangeably to mean the same thing. But writers often distinguish person from hypostasis, using "person" for the relation of certain things to one another. Even ordinary usage knows this meaning of "person." We say that someone has taken on my person, or that someone brought a lawsuit in another's person, and we say that the prefect bears the person of the emperor. This is why the adherents of Nestorius' doctrines will not say that there is either one nature or one hypostasis in Christ, since they do not hold a union of the hypostases themselves. Instead, they suppose that the one born of Mary is a mere man, who held the whole divine illumination within himself and differs from others only in that the divine illumination came to each of them more partially. Nevertheless they boldly insist that the person of Christ is one. By "one person" they mean the relation of God the Word to the man from Mary, since that man carried out the whole divine economy in the person of the Godhead of God the Word. On this basis they say that an insult against the man is rightly referred to God, just as the honour and insult that subjects pay the prefect are referred to the emperor himself. They say that the name "Christ" also

indicates this relation. That is why they see fit to call him one Christ: the relation, as has been said, is one, even if those who share in it are more than one. I think it is clear, then, to those who are devout about the Saviour's incarnation that, when we say the person of Christ is one, we do not use the term "person" for the mere relation of God to the man, as Nestorius' friends thought. Rather, we speak of the person of Christ in the way we speak of the one hypostasis of a man, say Peter or Paul. Let this point also be set out beforehand with the rest. It is true that Christ's humanity did not subsist without union with the Word for even the briefest moment, but received the beginning of its passage into being and its union with the Word at one and the same time. Yet we do not say that that nature was without hypostasis [?]. It had an existence that was self-subsistent in relation to other men and circumscribed in itself, distinguished by certain properties from the common nature of all the others. That, as we have just shown, is what the term "hypostasis" signifies. Therefore, just as we confess both a nature and a hypostasis in Christ's Godhead, so in his humanity we must confess this particular hypostasis as well as the nature. Otherwise, as I have said, we would be forced to call that nature without hypostasis. One thing is clear: the Saviour's humanity was one of the individuals belonging to the common nature. With these points thus clearly settled, and, I think, agreed by all, let those who hold that Christ's natures are two but his hypostasis one give us an answer. Each of the things united necessarily had both a nature and a hypostasis, as the argument has shown. Do they then confess that the natures and the hypostases were united in equal measure? Or do they think the hypostases were more united, since one hypostasis of both resulted, and the natures less, so that they remained two after the union? And after some other matters, in which he argues that substance does not admit of more and less, he says again: That one nature [?] belongs to several hypostases is, I think, evident to everyone. Thus we confess that the nature of the Godhead is one and hold that its hypostases are three. The nature of men, too, is one, while the hypostases under it extend almost to infinity in number, and the same holds for the rest. But it is impossible for two natures that keep their numerical duality to make up one hypostasis. This can be confirmed not only by induction from particular cases (how could there be one hypostasis of stone and wood,

that is, one individual, or of an ox and a horse?), but also from the very force of the argument. If each nature receives its existence in hypostases (which is the same as saying in individuals), then where there are two natures there must be at least two hypostases as well, in which the natures received their existence. For a nature cannot subsist by itself without being seen in some individual, and we have just shown that individual and hypostasis are the same. So those who say that through the union not only the hypostasis but also the nature became one are evidently consistent both with themselves and with the truth. But those who say that the hypostasis is one and the natures two are evidently inconsistent both with themselves and with the truth. "But," they say, "Christ's humanity had its hypostasis in the Word and did not subsist before the union with the Word; that is why we say that Christ's hypostasis is one." Then we in turn would ask: Do you take nature and hypostasis to signify one and the same thing, so that they are merely different names for one meaning, like "blade" and "sword"? Or do they mean different things? If they are the same, then since the hypostasis is one, the nature must also be one, just as, if the sword is one, the blade must also be one. Or if the natures are two, the hypostases will necessarily be two. Suppose instead that the term "nature" signifies one thing and "hypostasis" another, and that they think Christ's hypostasis is one because the man's hypostasis, that is, his person, did not exist before the union with the Word. Then surely the reason Christ's natures are two would be that the man's nature existed before the union with the Word [?]. But if the particular nature united to the Word subsisted beforehand, then its hypostasis must also have subsisted beforehand. Neither of these can exist without the other; I mean the particular nature cannot exist without its own hypostasis [?]. For both are one in the subject, even if those who use the terms often treat them as the same, as we showed a little earlier. If, then, the nature united to the Word, like the hypostasis, did not subsist before its union with him, let them claim that his nature is one for the very same reason they claim that Christ's hypostasis is one. Since it does not differ in respect of being united, neither in this respect would

[?] of the Halicarnassian, and of Gaianus of Alexandria; they are also called Gaianites. They agree in all other respects with the followers of Severus but differ from them on one point. The Severans seem to speak of a difference in the union of Christ, whereas these hold that the Lord's body was incorruptible from its very formation. We endure them by natural necessity, but Christ, they say, endured them voluntarily and was not subject to the laws of nature. 85. Agnoetae, also called Themistians. They impiously proclaim that Christ does not know the day of judgment, and they ascribe fear to him. They are an offshoot of the Theodosians, for Themistius, who became their heresiarch, held that there is one composite nature in Christ. 86. Barsanuphites, also called Semidalites. They are of one mind with the Gaianites and Theodosians, but go somewhat further. They add fine flour to what Dioscorus supposedly offered, touch it with a fingertip and taste the flour, and receive this in place of the mystery, making no offering at all. Having received [?], as has been said, the remains of Dioscorus' communion, they add fine flour whenever it has been used up little by little, and they count this as communion. 87. Hicetae. They are ascetics and orthodox in all other respects, but they gather together with women ascetics and offer hymns to God

with a kind of choral dancing, as if imitating the chorus of those who in Moses' time rose up together over the destruction of the Egyptians in the Red Sea. 88. Gnosimachi. They oppose all knowledge in Christianity, saying that those who seek out knowledge in the divine Scriptures are doing something superfluous. God, they say, asks nothing of a Christian but good deeds, so it is better to walk more simply and not to busy oneself with any doctrine that involves gnostic study. 89. Heliotropites. They say that the plants called heliotropes, which turn round with the rays of the sun, have a divine power that causes this turning in them, and so they want to honour them. They do not understand that this movement is something natural. 90 [?]. Thnetopsychites. They make the human soul like that of beasts and say that it perishes together with the body. 91 [?]. Agonyclites. They refuse to bend the knee at any time of prayer and always pray standing. 92 [?]. Theocatagnostae, also called blasphemers [?]. In certain words and deeds they try to find fault with God [?], with the holy persons dedicated to him and with the divine Scriptures; they are reckless and blasphemous people.

93 [?]. Christolytae. They say that after his resurrection from the dead our Lord Jesus Christ left his ensouled body below and ascended into heaven with his Godhead alone. 94. Ethnophrones. They follow the customs of the pagans, though they are Christians in other respects. They bring in birth-fate, fortune and destiny, and accept all astronomy and astrology, every kind of divination and the reading of birds. They impiously give themselves to auguries, averting rites [?], omens from chance words, the reading of portents, incantations and similar fables, and to the rest of pagan custom. They honour certain Greek festivals and also observe days, months, seasons and years. 95 [?]. Donatists: named after a certain Donatus in

…having begun in Africa, they hold in their hand a bone from the one who handed it over to them; they first kiss this, and only then partake of the offering of the holy gifts, when these are about to be brought forward. 96. Ethicoproscoptae: those who stumble in ethics, that is, in practical conduct. They disparage some of its teachings that are praiseworthy, and pursue as good some that are blameworthy. 97. Parermeneutae: those who misinterpret certain passages of the divine Scriptures, both of the Old and of the New Testament, and twist them to their own purpose. They are contentiously set against the many accurate and irreproachable interpretations. They suffer this from a certain lack of learning and lack of discernment, not knowing that they thereby confirm some of the heretical doctrines. 98. Lampetians: so called after a certain Lampetius. To those who wish to live together and spend their life in monastic communities they allow each one to pursue whatever way of life he wishes and approves, and to wear whatever habit he chooses. For the Christian, he says, should do nothing under compulsion, since it is written, "Willingly will I sacrifice to you," and again, "By my own will I will confess him." They also allow, as some say, giving room to the natural passions and not resisting them,

since nature so requires; and they are said to hold certain other views similar to those of the so-called Arians. [From these a certain [?] appeared, from whom come the Eustathians.] These heresies lasted until the times of Heraclius. From Heraclius until now the following have sprung up: 99. Monothelites: they took their beginning from Cyrus of Alexandria and were confirmed by Sergius of Constantinople. They proclaim two natures in Christ and one hypostasis, but teach one will and one operation, thereby abolishing the duality of the natures and clinging strongly to the doctrines of Apollinaris. [100. Autoproscoptae: though orthodox in every respect, they boldly cut themselves off from the catholic Church and its communion on some trivial pretext. They claim to be seeking the canonical rules, yet they are neither bishops nor in any way leaders of the people, but some of the common herd; and they themselves stumble in the very things of which they accuse others. For they openly live with women and gather "spiritual sisters" into their houses; they busy themselves with trade, with greed and with other worldly affairs; and they live unreasonably, overturning in deed what they claim in word to uphold, being transgressors, according to the apostle's verdict. For while honoring God in word, they dishonor him in deed, though they are monks and enrolled in the clergy. Those who are dazzled by them follow them, walking in their simplicity. (Rom. 2:25)

But the true nurslings of the Church revere the holy canons; and while leaving what concerns them to bishops and leaders, they themselves cherish them earnestly in deed, defending [?] them through good order.] 101. There is also the superstition of the Ishmaelites, deceiver of peoples, which prevails to this day and is the forerunner of the Antichrist. It derives from Ishmael, who was born to Abraham of Hagar; for this reason they are called Hagarenes and Ishmaelites. They are also called Saracens, as being "empty of Sarah," because Hagar said to the angel, "Sarah has sent me away empty." These people practised idolatry and worshipped the morning star and Aphrodite, whom in their own language they named Chabar, which means "great." Until the times of Heraclius they were openly idolaters. From that time until now a false prophet has arisen among them, [Variant reading: Chaber. [?] Mohammed.]

called Mamed. He came across the Old and New Testaments and likewise, it seems, conversed with an Arian monk, and so put together a heresy of his own. Having won the nation over by a show of piety, he spreads the report that a scripture was brought down to him from heaven. So, having set down in his book certain compositions worthy of laughter, he hands this down [?] to them as the object of their worship. He says that there is one God, maker of all things, neither begotten nor begetting. He says that Christ is the Word of God and his Spirit, but created and a servant, and that he was born without seed of Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron. For the Word of God, he says, and the Spirit entered into Mary, and she gave birth to Jesus, a prophet and servant of God. He also says that the Jews, acting lawlessly, wanted to crucify him, and having seized him they crucified his shadow; but Christ himself, he says, was neither crucified nor did he die, for God took him to himself into heaven because he loved him. And he says this: that when Christ had gone up into the heavens, God questioned him, saying, "O Jesus, did you say, 'I am the Son of God, and God'?" And Jesus, he says, answered, "Be merciful to me, Lord. You know that I did not say it, nor do I scorn to be your servant. But sinful men wrote that I said this, and they lied against me, and they are in error." And God answered, he says, and said to him, "I know that you did not say this." He tells many other marvels worthy of laughter in this composition, and boasts that it was brought down to him from God. But we say, "And who is it that bears witness that God gave him a scripture? And which of the prophets foretold that such a prophet would arise?" When they are at a loss, we point out that Moses received the law on Mount Sinai while God appeared in the sight of all the people, in cloud and fire and darkness and storm. We point out too that all the prophets, from Moses onward, foretold the coming of Christ: that Christ is God and that the Son of God will come in the flesh, will be crucified, will die and will rise again, and that he is the judge of the living and the dead. And we say, "How is it that your prophet did not come in this way, with others bearing witness about him? And why did God not give him the scripture you speak of in your presence, as he gave the law to Moses while the people looked on and the mountain smoked, so that you too might have certainty?" They answer that God does whatever he wills. "This too

we know," we say, "but what we are asking is how the scripture came down to your prophet." And they answer that the scripture came down upon him while he was asleep. Then we say to them the laughable thing: since he received the scripture while asleep and did not perceive its working, the popular proverb has been fulfilled in him: [?]… Again we ask, "Since he commanded you in your scripture to do nothing and accept nothing without witnesses, how is it that you did not ask him, 'First prove by witness that you are a prophet and that you have come from God; and what scripture bears witness about you?'" Then they fall silent for shame. "You may not marry a wife without witnesses, nor buy, nor acquire property; and you yourselves will not accept a donkey or any beast without a witness. Your wives, your possessions, your donkeys and everything else you have through witnesses. Only your faith and your scripture you hold without a witness. For the one who handed this scripture down to you has no confirmation from anywhere, nor is anyone known who bore witness to him beforehand; on the contrary, he received it while asleep." They call us Hetaeriasts, that is, "Associators," because, they say, we introduce an associate alongside God by saying that Christ is the Son of God and God. To them we say that this is what the prophets and the Scripture have handed down, and you, as you insist, accept the prophets. If then we are wrong to call Christ the Son of God, they are the ones who taught it and handed it down to us. Some of them say that we have added such things by allegorizing the prophets. Others say that the Hebrews, out of hatred for us, deceived us by writing these things as though they came from the prophets, so that we might perish. Again we say to them: "Since you say that Christ is the Word and Spirit of God, how is it that you revile us as Associators? For the word and the spirit are inseparable from the one in whom they naturally exist. If, then, his Word is in God, clearly he is also God. But if he is outside God, then according to you God is without word and without spirit. So in fleeing from giving God an associate, you have mutilated him. It would have been better for you to say that he has an associate than to mutilate him and present him as a stone or a piece of wood or some other senseless thing. So you, speaking falsely of us, call us Associators; but we call you the Mutilators
of God." [?] They also accuse us of being idolaters because we venerate the cross, which they abhor. And we say

to them: "How is it, then, that you rub yourselves against a stone at your Chabatha [?], and show your love for the stone by kissing it?" Some of them say that Abraham lay with Hagar upon it; others, that he tied his camel to it when he was about to sacrifice Isaac. And we answer them: "Scripture says that the mountain was wooded and had trees, from which Abraham split wood for the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac, and that he left the donkeys behind with the servants. Where, then, do you get your nonsense? For there are no forest trees in that place, nor do donkeys pass that way." They are ashamed, yet they still say that the stone is Abraham's. Then we say: "Let it be Abraham's, as you foolishly claim. Are you not ashamed to kiss it merely because Abraham lay with a woman on it, or because he tied a camel to it, while you blame us for venerating the cross of Christ, through which the power of the demons and the deceit of the devil have been destroyed?" This stone they speak of is in fact the head of Aphrodite, whom they used to worship and whom they called Chaber; and even now the trace of a carving can be seen on it by those who look carefully. This Mamed, as has been said, composed many absurdities and gave each of them a title. For example, there is the scripture of The Woman, in which he plainly legislates that a man may take four wives, and concubines too, if he can, a thousand, as many as his hand can hold in subjection besides the four wives. He also allows a man to divorce whichever wife he wishes, if he so wishes, and take another. He made this law for the following reason. Mamed had a companion named Zeid. This man had a beautiful wife, and Mamed fell in love with her. While they were sitting together, Mamed said, "So-and-so, God has commanded me to take your wife." And he answered, "You are an apostle. Do as God has told you: take my wife." Or rather, to tell the story from the beginning, he said to him, "God has commanded me that you should divorce your wife." And he divorced her. And many days later he said, "But God has also commanded that I take her." Then, having taken her and committed adultery with her, he laid down this law: "Whoever wishes may divorce his wife. But if after divorcing her he wants to return to her, let another man marry her first. For it is not lawful to take her back unless she has been married by another. And if a brother divorces his wife, let his brother marry her, if he wishes." In this same scripture he gives such precepts as these. Again there is the scripture of The Camel of God. About it he says that there was a camel from God which drank a whole river and could not pass between two mountains, because there was not

room enough for it. There was a people in that place, he says, and on one day they drank the water, and the camel drank it on the next. And by drinking the water the camel nourished them, supplying them with milk in place of the water. Then those men, being wicked, he says, rose up and killed the camel. But it had an offspring, a little camel, which, he says, cried out to God when its mother was killed, and God took it to himself. We say to them: "Where did that camel come from?" And they say, "From God." And we say, "Did another camel mate with it?" And they say, "No." "How, then," we say, "did it give birth? For we see that your camel is without father, without mother and without genealogy; and having given birth, it came to harm. Yet the one that mated with it is nowhere to be seen, and the little camel was taken up. Why, then, did your prophet, to whom, as you say, God spoke, not learn about the camel, where it grazes and who gets milk by milking it? Or perhaps it too fell among wicked men like its mother and was killed? Or did it enter paradise before you as your forerunner, so that from it you will have the river of milk you prattle about? For you say that three rivers flow for you in paradise: of water, of wine and of milk. If your forerunner the camel is outside paradise, clearly it has withered away from hunger and thirst, or others will enjoy its milk; and your prophet boasts in vain of having conversed with God, since the mystery of the camel was not revealed to him. But if it is in paradise, it will drink up the water again, and you will be parched for lack of water in the midst of the delights of paradise. And if, there being no water (for the camel drank it all), you long for wine from the river flowing by, you will drink it unmixed and be inflamed, and stagger with drunkenness and fall asleep. Then, heavy-headed after your sleep and hung over from the wine, you will forget the pleasures of paradise. How, then, did your prophet not foresee that these things might befall you in the paradise of delight? He never gave a thought to the camel and where it now dwells. Nor did you ask him, when he told you of the three rivers he had dreamed up. But we tell you plainly that your wonderful camel has gone ahead of you into the souls of donkeys, where you too, being like beasts, are destined to dwell. There is the outer darkness and the endless punishment, the roaring fire, the sleepless worm and the demons of Tartarus." Again Mamed speaks of the scripture of The Table. He says that Christ asked God for a table and it was given to him. For God, he says, said to him, "I have given you and yours a table
[?]." Again he speaks of the scripture of The Heifer, and some other nonsense worthy of laughter, which because of its quantity I think I must pass

over. He legislated that they be circumcised, women as well as men. He commanded them neither to keep the Sabbath nor to be baptized. He taught them to eat some of the things forbidden in the law and to abstain from others, and he forbade wine-drinking altogether. 102. Christianocategori, that is, "Accusers of Christians": they are and are called this because they accused Christians, who worship one living and true God praised in Trinity, of worshipping as gods, as the pagans do, the venerable icons of our Lord Jesus Christ, of our immaculate Lady the holy Theotokos, of the holy angels and of his saints. They are called Iconoclasts because, displaying a disposition that dishonors all, they smashed these same holy and venerable icons and gave them to the fire. Likewise, of the images on the walls, some they scraped off and others they defaced with lime and black paint. They are called Thymoleontes, "Wrathful Lions," because, seizing their opportunity when they held power and arming their heresy with wrath, they punished without measure, with tortures and torments, those who accepted the icons. They also took a name from the heresiarch [?].
